en: A Brief Discussion on the Heart Sutra, composed by Ming Guanheng.
Regarding the title of this sutra, "Mahāprajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra," these ten characters constitute the name of the scripture. Mahā...
*Ha* is a Sanskrit term; in the language of Tang (Chinese), it means "great. *Prajñā* is a Sanskrit term; in the language of Tang, it means "wisdom. *Pāramitā* is a Sanskrit term;

in the language of Tang, it means "reaching the other shore," which is to say, reaching the further shore. This refers to the fact that sentient beings lack wisdom and thus wander in delusion within the ocean of suffering of birth and death.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess great wisdom, which illuminates and shatters ignorance, enabling them to transcend birth and death.
The ocean of suffering. To reach the other shore of nirvāṇa is why it is called *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. Regarding the single character "mind" (*xin*):
if one contemplates it as being above, it is the mind of *prajñā*; if one contemplates it as being below, this root scripture is the "mind" of its six hundred fascicles.
"Sūtra" is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "Kie-king" (契經). It refers to a teaching that accords with principle and accords with the capacities of sentient beings.
This region [China] abbreviates these [prefixes]. Therefore, it is simply called a *sūtra*.

Thus, it is titled the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* (in this sūtra, the term *mahā* is often not read; according to the text itself which speaks of "profound *prajñā*," the title should likewise include "Great *Prajñā*").
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva is one who is able to practice Prajñāpāramitā; this person is cited here to manifest the Dharma of Prajñāpāramitā.
The three characters "Avalokiteśvara" are the specific name of this Bodhisattva, while the two characters "Bodhisattva" are his general title.
Why is he called Avalokiteśvara? It is said that when this Bodhisattva practices the profound Prajñāpāramitā, he contemplates and perceives the five [aggregates]...

The aggregates are all empty; having transcended all suffering and calamity, he is therefore named Avalokiteśvara. To clearly perceive that the five aggregates are all empty is "contemplation" (*guan*);
to transcend all suffering and calamity is "sovereignty" (*zizai*). The above briefly explains the general meaning of the three characters [Avalokiteśvara];
below, their significance will be further elucidated. "Śāriputra" is the name of this Venerable One. As this Venerable One is foremost in wisdom, his name is invoked.
And he bestowed it upon him, saying: "As stated above, one perceives that the five aggregates are all empty. How does one perceive this? How does one attain emptiness?
Śāriputra, you should contemplate and observe in this way: form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form; form is itself emptiness."
"Emptiness is form. To contemplate in this way is precisely emptiness. Regarding these four phrases: the first two phrases first illuminate that the substance of form and emptiness are one;
the latter two phrases then illuminate that the nature of form is fundamentally empty. To say they are "not different" is intended to establish the subsequent word "is" (i.e., *ji*).
In sum, the phrase "form is emptiness" is the primary point, while the others serve as supportive elements. This refers to the single dharma of form.
One contemplates and observes in this manner. One contemplates and observes feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness in the same way; therefore, it is said, "it is also thus.
The first part explained that the five aggregates are all empty.

The second part explains "crossing over all suffering and calamity," meaning that if the dharmas of the five aggregates were to exist, they would possess the characteristic of arising, the characteristic of ceasing, the characteristic of defilement, the characteristic of purity, the characteristic of increase, and the characteristic of decrease.
[Their] characteristics are all the characteristic of suffering. If all phenomena have the characteristic of emptiness, and since they have the characteristic of emptiness, what is there to arise?
What is there to cease? What is there to be defiled? What is there to be pure? What is there to increase? What is there to decrease?

Since there is neither arising nor ceasing, nor defilement nor purity, and so forth, this is the true bliss of nirvāṇa. Therefore, he further addressed Śāriputra: "This emptiness-characteristic of all phenomena is neither born nor does it perish."
"Neither defiled nor pure; neither increasing nor decreasing. This section explains the preceding phrase, "crossing over all suffering and calamity.
Having already explained the meaning of "clearly seeing that the five aggregates are all empty, thereby crossing over all suffering and calamity," the following provides a detailed exposition.
Therefore, the phrase "within emptiness" refers back to the aforementioned "mark of the emptiness of all phenomena" and speaks of this.
In emptiness, it is not only that the five aggregates are empty; the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are also empty, and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are also empty.
There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; there is no form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental object. This is the emptiness of the twelve bases.

There is no eye-element, and so on, up to no mind-consciousness-element. This is the emptiness of the eighteen elements. This is the emptiness of worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*). Below is the emptiness of...
Regarding supramundane dharmas: there is no ignorance, up to and including no extinction of ignorance; there is no old age and death, up to and including no extinction of old age and death.
This is the emptiness of the pratyekabuddha-dharma. There is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; there is no wisdom and no attainment. This is the emptiness of the śrāvaka-dharma.
It is said that within this emptiness, both the mundane and the supramundane are empty. This is the exposition of the above.
The phrase "to perceive that the five aggregates are all empty" constitutes the single character of "contemplation.
The phrase "because there is nothing to be attained" is a term that承接 (links) what precedes and initiates what follows; it means that both mundane and supramundane dharmas are entirely unattainable.
Because there is nothing to be attained, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas rely upon this to sever afflictions, realize bodhi, transcend birth and death, and attain [nirvana].
Nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is called *bodhisattva*. By relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, the mind is without hindrance.
Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear. One is far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, attaining ultimate nirvāṇa.
This means that the bodhisattvas rely on *prajñā* to leave suffering behind and attain bliss. The Buddhas of the three periods of time rely on the *prajñāpāramitā*.
For this reason, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This statement means that all Buddhas rely on *prajñā* to transcend suffering and attain bliss.

From "by means of non-attainment" up to "attaining *anuttara-bodhi*"—this section elaborates upon and provides scriptural evidence for the preceding phrase, "crossing over all suffering and distress," which refers precisely to the two characters "sovereignty" (*svatantra*). Having already analyzed and explained the preceding portion:

This section clarifies the exposition and the citation of evidence. It clarifies that the place where one realizes and perceives that the five aggregates are all empty, thereby transcending all suffering and calamity, is the true locus.
Therefore, the conclusion below is established in two parts. First, it concludes by manifesting the merit of Prajñāpāramitā; thus it says:

"Therefore, know that Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra" (transforming the ordinary into the holy, its spiritual subtlety is unfathomable); "it is a great illuminating mantra" (the sun of wisdom hangs in the sky, shattering the darkness of ignorance); "it is..."

The unsurpassed mantra; (unsurpassed because there is nothing before it and nothing added above it). This is the unequaled mantra; (it is not only unsurpassed, but there is also nothing equal to it). The first section concludes by manifesting the divine efficacy of Prajñā. The second section forms the introduction to the subject (*pratīka*).
Following the previous refutation which stated, "To perceive that the five aggregates are all empty is to transcend all suffering and calamity," one might ask:
how is this to be seen? Since the exposition has already been clarified, elaborated, and supported with citations until it is perfectly clear, for this reason—
The conclusion states: "It is able to eliminate all suffering; it is true and not false. This is precisely *Svayambhū* (the Self-Existent).
In sum, this entire sutra is exhausted by the three characters "Guanshiyin" (Avalokiteśvara). The preceding was the explicit teaching; the following is the esoteric teaching.
Therefore, he speaks the *Prajñāpāramitā* mantra. He then spoke the mantra, saying: *Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate*.
*Saṃgate bodhi svāhā*. The exoteric explanation causes people to give rise to wisdom by relying on the meaning;
the esoteric explanation causes people to give rise to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) through recitation. When concentration and wisdom are equal, the practice is complete.
A Brief Discussion on the Heart Sutra (Concluded)
